description: Solo builder from Ottawa (Maksym Stepanenko), joining the Ottawa event online via Discord. Challenge: Lunar Landing Site Navigator.
summary: Dawnline is a browser tool for choosing a lunar landing site and a landing date by light and by contact with Earth. Near the south pole the Sun circles about 1.5 degrees above or below the horizon, so a crater rim 20 km away can hide it for days. For 45 sites, from the Shackleton connecting ridge to the Apollo and Chang'e landings, Dawnline traces the real Sun and Earth over each site's measured skyline, built from NASA LRO LOLA elevation data with 720 rays out to 250 km. For any landing day from 15 Nov 2026 to 14 Nov 2027 and a mission from 7 days to one year, it reports sunlight, solar energy, the longest night, Earth in view for direct-to-Earth radio, and the longest blackout. A 360-degree horizon view plays the mission hour by hour, a compare view shows a whole year of landing days per site, and anyone can tap the pole map to trace a new site's horizon in the browser. Every Sun and Earth position is checked against NASA JPL Horizons: the largest difference is 0.0026 degrees. Open source under Apache-2.0.
details:
Live app: https://dawnline.mmix.biz . Code: https://github.com/ctmakc/dawnline (Apache-2.0). Demo video: https://dawnline.mmix.biz/demo.mp4 (28 s screen recording of the live app).

What it does. Dawnline answers one question for a lunar landing: if we land here on this day, how much sunlight and how much contact with Earth do we get? Pick one of 45 sites or tap the south-pole map, choose a landing day and a mission length (7 days, 14 days, one lunar day, 90 days or one year). The app shows the sunlit share of the solar disk, solar energy in kWh/m2 for a sun-tracking panel, the longest night, the share of hours with Earth in view, and the longest blackout.

How it works. A Python pipeline reads NASA LRO LOLA gridded elevation models from the PDS: polar LDEM at 20, 40, 80 and 240 m and the global LDEM_16. For each site it casts 720 great-circle rays, one every 0.5 degrees, out to 250 km from a 2 m mast, and keeps the highest terrain angle with lunar curvature. In the browser, a web worker computes the Sun and Earth directions for 17,544 hours with astronomy-engine and the IAU Moon rotation model. The visible fraction of the solar disk is measured against the skyline every hour, and prefix sums let any landing day and mission window be read at once. A pin dropped on the map gets its horizon traced in the browser from a 400 m terrain tile.

Validation. We pulled airless apparent azimuth and elevation from NASA JPL Horizons for 5 sites at 8 times each, 80 site-hours in all. The largest difference is 0.0026 degrees for the Sun and 0.0023 degrees for Earth, under 1% of the solar disk. The check table and the raw JSON are on the page.

Benefits and impact. Near the pole, terrain shadows that move through the year decide the landing date. Dawnline makes that visible to anyone with a browser. A planner can compare the Shackleton connecting ridge with the de Gerlache rim in seconds, a teacher can show why a site 20 km away sits in darkness, and a student can test a site of their own. Each site in the compare view gets a strip of 365 landing days, so the best window stands out at a glance.

Tools. TypeScript, React and Vite for the app; Canvas 2D for the horizon panorama, the mission timeline and the date strips; a web worker for the ephemeris; Python with numpy and Pillow for the terrain pipeline; astronomy-engine for positions; JPL Horizons for the check. Fonts: Jost and Space Mono (open licence). It is a static site that works on a phone at 390 px and on desktop.

Creativity. The horizon view draws the Sun and Earth paths over a 360-degree skyline, so you watch terrain hide them while a mission timeline plays. The pole map is shaded with cast shadows from the computed Sun direction. The compare strips turn a year of landing days into one picture per site.

What we took into account. The Moon has no air, so there is no refraction to model. We leave out local slope, boulders, the lander's own shadow and dust on panels, and the mast height is fixed at 2 m. Map pins use a coarser grid and can miss small nearby ridges. Rounded or proxy coordinates are flagged in each site's source note. Dawnline is meant for comparison and teaching; mission operations need full-resolution terrain and a team check.

Use of AI (Super Intelligence) tools. We built Dawnline with an AI coding assistant, Claude Code by Anthropic. It was used for research of sources, the code, the data pipeline, the interface design, the written text and the scripted screen recording. A human chose the theme and the challenge and reviewed the work. Every number comes from LOLA terrain and astronomy-engine and is checked against JPL Horizons. No image, video, audio or data in the project was AI-generated: the map and panoramas are rendered from LOLA elevation data, and the demo video is a screen recording of the app. The same note is in the app's Method section and in the README. No NASA logos or branding are used.
dataRefs: LRO LOLA Gridded Data Records (polar LDEM 20/40/80/240 m, global LDEM_16), NASA PDS Geosciences Node
NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris system (validation of Sun and Earth positions)
LROC anthropogenic objects table, LRO Camera (landed hardware positions, Wagner et al. 2017)
Glaser et al. 2018, illumination of the lunar south pole (NASA NTRS 20170007365)
NASA, update on Moon base rovers, landers and missions (Shackleton connecting ridge)
projectRefs: astronomy-engine by D. Cross, MIT licence (Sun, Earth and Moon orientation)
Wueller et al. 2026, JGR Planets, Artemis III candidate site points (Table A1)
Bussey et al. 2010, Icarus 208, illumination near the lunar south pole
IAU / USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature (crater and massif centres)
Claude Code by Anthropic, AI coding assistant used to build the project
Open-source libraries: React, Vite, TypeScript, numpy, Pillow, Jost and Space Mono fonts (full list in the repository)
